_meta.purpose: PROPOSAL ONLY -- not the live library. Demonstrates an extended entry schema for prompts/meme_library.DRAFT.json on ONE comedic-engine cluster (drake, distracted-boyfriend, left-exit-12-off-ramp), plus one deliberate contrast template (two-buttons) that sits in the same category but a DIFFERENT engine. Review the shape here before it is applied to all 30 templates.
_meta.why_this_exists: The v1 library documented template MECHANICS (which panel is which) but omitted the three things that make a meme land: who it is about, where the laugh comes from, and the required valence relationship between boxes. On drake the v1 entry had the valence INVERTED -- it described box 1 as the smarter/preferred option, when the joke requires box 1 to be the worse option the subject actually chose. That error would actively steer the writer toward earnest, non-funny memes.

new_fields.engine: Cluster key. Templates sharing a comedic engine share their comedic_engine, valence_rule, choice_state and failure_mode, defined once under _meta.engines. Lets ~30 templates be fixed as ~5-7 clusters instead of 30 independent rewrites, and keeps sibling templates consistent with each other.
new_fields.subject: Who the meme is ABOUT -- the person/team/org whose decision or reaction is the joke. placement is one of: 'implied' (no box; name them in surrounding copy), 'box:N' (a physical panel labels the subject), or 'none' (subjectless template). v1 had no subject concept at all, which is why its entries produced abstract comparisons with no protagonist.
new_fields.comedic_engine: One sentence on where the laugh actually comes from -- almost always a violated expectation.
new_fields.valence: The REQUIRED relationship between boxes, stated as a rule a writer can be caught violating. This is the checkable part.
new_fields.worked_example: A concrete, correctly-shaped example. One example teaches an LLM more than three sentences of description.
new_fields.anti_example: The plausible near-miss that fails -- usually the earnest/flat version. Exists to stop regression toward the engine's failure_mode.

_meta.examples_are_illustrative: IMPORTANT: worked_example and anti_example captions demonstrate SHAPE ONLY. They are not factual claims and must never be reused as source material or treated as true. Real captions must be built from game_state.json ground truth.
open_questions_for_review: engine vs pattern_type -- kept here as two separate axes: engine = shared comedic mechanism, pattern_type = structural caption-to-panel mapping. drake and left-exit share BOTH; distracted-boyfriend shares the engine but has a different pattern_type (it labels the subject in a box). Keep both axes, or collapse to one?

distracted-boyfriend box_count -- this proposal says 3 per review feedback, but prompts/meme_reference.txt lists it under '2 panels' and generate_memes.py _expand_boxes() has no case for it, so the pipeline currently sends only 2 captions and the subject panel likely renders uncaptioned. Needs verification against a real Imgflip render; may require a code + reference fix, not just metadata.
Should status stay a flat candidate/verified, or split into semantics_reviewed vs example_reviewed? The box semantics and the worked examples are separately reviewable.
Are worked_example captions worth carrying at all, given they must never be reused as fact? Alternative is shape-only skeletons with no real names.

subject_abandons_sensible_for_funky.summary: A named subject faces an obviously correct option and visibly goes with the worse, pettier, or stranger one.
subject_abandons_sensible_for_funky.comedic_engine: The laugh is not the comparison itself -- it is that a real, named person actually chose the dumb thing, while the audience can plainly see the right answer.
subject_abandons_sensible_for_funky.valence_rule: The abandoned option MUST be genuinely appealing or rational. The chosen option MUST be petty, self-defeating, or conspicuously odd. NEVER write the chosen option as the smarter one.
subject_abandons_sensible_for_funky.choice_state: already made -- the subject has committed and we are reacting to it
subject_abandons_sensible_for_funky.failure_mode: The straight upgrade: both options ranked with the second genuinely better. Produces an earnest endorsement or an ad, with zero comedy.

forced_choice_dilemma.summary: A subject is frozen between two options of the SAME valence -- both appealing, or both painful -- that cannot coexist.
forced_choice_dilemma.comedic_engine: The paralysis is the joke, not the options. Either the audience finds the answer obvious and the subject clearly does not, or the two buttons expose a hypocrisy the subject created themselves.
forced_choice_dilemma.valence_rule: The two options MUST be same-valence and genuinely in conflict. If one is clearly better there is no sweat and the meme dies.
forced_choice_dilemma.choice_state: not yet made -- the subject is still sweating
forced_choice_dilemma.failure_mode: Writing it as a ranked preference. That is the abandons-sensible engine wearing the wrong template.

_meta.scope: 4 of 30 templates, for shape review only. template_id values remain inherited from CURATED_TEMPLATES in generate_memes.py and are unchanged.

subject.who: The person, team, or front office making the choice.
subject.note: Drake is the stand-in for the subject. Name them in the surrounding paragraph -- the boxes carry the two options only.

templates.comedic_engine: A named figure had the obvious move available and went with the pettier one instead.
templates.valence: Box 0 MUST be the obviously desirable/rational thing. Box 1 MUST be the petty, self-defeating, or odd thing the subject actually chose. Never write box 1 as the smarter option -- that inverts the joke into an endorsement.

boxes.purpose: the sensible, obviously appealing option the subject is waving off
boxes.valence: positive -- must read as the right answer

boxes.purpose: the petty or self-defeating option the subject is actually going with
boxes.valence: negative or absurd -- must read as the wrong answer they picked anyway

templates.use_when: A specific, named figure passed on the obvious move and chose something pettier, stranger, or plainly worse -- and that choice is already public.
templates.do_not_use_when: No specific subject is making the choice, or box 1 is genuinely the better option. A ranked upgrade with no bad decision is an ad, not a joke.

worked_example.subject: Jeanie Buss
boxes: SELLING THE LAKERS FOR $2B MORE A YEAR LATER
worked_example.why_it_lands: Box 0 is the rational windfall anyone would take. Box 1 is the pettiness she chose instead. The subject is named in the copy, not in a box.

boxes: READING ABOUT IT IN SLAP THE NEXT DAY
anti_example.why_it_fails: Straight upgrade, no subject, nobody makes a bad decision -- it reads as an ad. This is the example currently sitting in prompts/meme_reference.txt, so the existing reference material is teaching the wrong instinct.

templates.note: AI-authored box semantics, not yet reviewed by Abram. Valence CORRECTED from v1 per review feedback -- v1 had box 1 as the better option.

templates.box_count_conflict: v1 said 2. Review feedback says 3, with the subject in box 2. prompts/meme_reference.txt lists this template under '2 panels' and generate_memes.py _expand_boxes() has no case for it, so the pipeline currently sends 2 captions and the subject panel likely renders uncaptioned. VERIFY against a real render before trusting this entry.

subject.who: The person or team doing the looking -- the one moving on.
subject.note: Unlike drake, the subject IS captioned here. That label is what makes the meme land; leaving it blank strands the joke.

templates.comedic_engine: The subject is visibly turning away, in public, from the thing they were committed to -- and everyone can see them doing it.
templates.valence: Box 0 MUST be the established commitment being left behind. Box 1 is the new object of attention -- it does NOT have to be worse than box 0, but it must be notable that the subject is moving on. Box 2 MUST name the subject doing the looking.

boxes.purpose: the established thing being neglected -- the prior commitment, incumbent, or plan
the new thing catching the subject's eye
boxes.valence: notable -- either worse, or simply surprising that they are moving on

boxes.purpose: the subject themselves -- the person or team doing the looking
boxes.valence: neutral -- this is a label, not a judgment

templates.use_when: A team or figure publicly moves on from an incumbent or prior commitment toward a new option, and the pivot itself is the story.
templates.do_not_use_when: Nobody is abandoning anything, or you cannot name the subject for box 2. Without the subject label this collapses into a generic two-way comparison -- use drake instead.

worked_example.subject: The Vikings
worked_example.why_it_lands: Box 0 is who they were committed to, box 1 is who they turned toward, box 2 names who is doing the turning.
worked_example.timing: Post-decision only -- runs after the starter call is public. Before the decision there is no abandonment to point at.

anti_example.why_it_fails: No subject, nobody doing the looking, and only 2 of 3 boxes filled. An abstract trend comparison, not a person visibly moving on.

templates.note: AI-authored box semantics, not yet reviewed by Abram. box_count raised 2 -> 3 per review feedback; see box_count_conflict -- needs verification against a real render.

subject.who: The person or team making the abrupt swerve.
subject.note: The car is the subject. SLAP uses 2 boxes, so name the subject in surrounding copy.

templates.comedic_engine: Same abandonment as drake, but the humor is in the VIOLENCE of the swerve -- this was not a considered preference, it was a last-second reflex nobody saw coming.
templates.valence: Box 0 MUST be the sensible route being blown past. Box 1 MUST be the impulsive exit taken instead. Same valence rule as drake -- box 1 is the worse option.

boxes.purpose: the sensible route straight ahead, being blown past
the impulsive exit the subject swerves toward at the last second
boxes.valence: negative or chaotic -- the reflex decision

templates.use_when: An abrupt, panicked, or deadline-driven decision that abandoned an established plan. Pick this over drake when the SUDDENNESS is the story.
templates.do_not_use_when: The decision was calm, gradual, or long-telegraphed -- that is drake. The tire-screech is the whole point here.

worked_example.subject: A front office at the trade deadline
boxes: RUN IT BACK WITH A HEALTHY ROSTER
TRADE THREE FIRSTS AN HOUR BEFORE THE DEADLINE
worked_example.why_it_lands: Box 0 is the plan they were already on; box 1 is the last-second swerve. The deadline timing is what earns this template over drake.
worked_example.timing: Best same-day as the abrupt move.

anti_example.why_it_fails: Two versions of the same calm plan. No swerve, no abruptness -- nothing for the template to do.

templates.note: AI-authored box semantics, not yet reviewed by Abram. Marked 'pretty good' in v1 review; refined here mainly to sharpen the drake-vs-left-exit boundary.

templates.included_as: CONTRAST CASE -- demonstrates that the engine axis has real boundaries. Same category as the three above, different engine.

subject.who: The person or team sweating the decision.
subject.note: The sweating figure is the subject. Name them in surrounding copy.

templates.comedic_engine: The paralysis is the joke -- not the options. Either the audience thinks the answer is obvious and the subject clearly does not, or the two buttons expose a hypocrisy the subject created themselves.
templates.valence: The two buttons MUST be the SAME valence -- both appealing, or both painful. If one is clearly better there is no sweat and the meme dies. Distinct from drake: here the choice has NOT been made yet.

boxes.purpose: the first button -- one horn of the dilemma
the second button -- the conflicting horn, cannot coexist with box 0

templates.use_when: A subject is visibly stuck between two options of equal weight that cannot both be taken -- especially when choosing either one exposes something about them.
templates.do_not_use_when: One option is clearly better (that is drake), or the choice is already made (also drake -- this template is for the sweat BEFORE the decision).

worked_example.subject: A GM after a bad trade
boxes: ADMIT THE TRADE WAS A MISTAKE
DOUBLE DOWN AND SEND ANOTHER FIRST
worked_example.why_it_lands: Both options are painful, they genuinely conflict, and the dilemma is entirely self-inflicted. No decision has been made yet -- he is still sweating.

anti_example.why_it_fails: Opposite valence and not a real dilemma -- nobody sweats over whether to win. A ranked preference wearing the wrong template.

templates.note: AI-authored box semantics, not yet reviewed by Abram. Same-valence requirement added per review feedback.
